# Hydrochloric acid and aqua regia (`hydrochloric_acid_aqua_regia`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: needs distillation; helped by sulphuric_acid, nitric_acid, salt_production
- Core idea: Common salt heated with oil of vitriol in a retort gives a choking gas that dissolves greedily in water to form spirit of salt (hydrochloric acid); the residue is Glauber's salt. It dissolves iron, zinc and tin, cleans metal for tinning and soldering, and is the same acid as in the stomach. One part nitric acid with three parts hydrochloric acid (or nitric acid with sal ammoniac dissolved in it) is aqua regia, the only common liquid that dissolves gold and platinum.
- Pitfalls:
  - The gas attacks eyes and lungs and rusts every iron tool in the room.
  - Mixing it with bleaching powder or pyrolusite releases chlorine.
  - Aqua regia cannot be stored in a stoppered bottle; it gives off gas and bursts it. Mix it fresh.
  - Expecting aqua regia to dissolve silver well; a crust of silver chloride stops the attack.
- History: islamic: 9th–10th c. – sal ammoniac and corrosive mixtures with salt and vitriol in al-Razi; isolation of the acid itself is disputed; europe: c. 1300 – aqua regia from nitric acid and sal ammoniac in pseudo-Geber; c. 1600 spirit of salt described by Libavius and in the Basil Valentine texts; 1648 Glauber's method from salt and oil of vitriol; 1772 Priestley collects the gas
- Read:
  - Johann Rudolf Glauber, Furni novi philosophici (1646–1649)
  - Robert P. Multhauf, The Origins of Chemistry (1966)
